reconstructed_theorem_text:
Let A and B be arbitrary types equipped with sigma-algebras. For every s-finite nonnegative measure mu on A, every s-finite measurable kernel R from A to B, and every s-finite measurable kernel F from A x B to B, the following implication holds. A measure is s-finite when it is a countable sum of finite measures; the kernel assumption is the analogous countable-sum condition for kernels. A kernel assigns nonnegative measures measurably and need not assign probability measures.

Suppose that for mu-almost every a in A the kernel F_a from B to B, defined by F_a(b) = F(a,b), is reversible with respect to the measure R(a). Explicitly, outside a single mu-null exceptional set of a-values, for every pair of measurable sets E and G in B, the integral over b in E of F(a,b)(G) with respect to R(a)(db) equals the integral over b in G of F(a,b)(E) with respect to R(a)(db). The exceptional set of a-values is independent of E and G.

Give A x B its product sigma-algebra. Define the joint measure pi = mu compProd R by requiring that the integral of every nonnegative measurable function h(a,b) against pi be the iterated integral of h(a,b), first against R(a)(db) and then against mu(da). Define the kernel K from A x B to A x B by K((a,b)) = delta_a x F(a,b), the product of the Dirac measure at a and the measure F(a,b). Thus its first output coordinate is the input coordinate a, while its second output coordinate is measured by F(a,b).

Then K is reversible with respect to pi: for every pair of measurable sets U and V in A x B, the integral over x in U of K(x)(V) with respect to pi(dx) equals the integral over x in V of K(x)(U) with respect to pi(dx). This conclusion concerns all measurable product-space sets U and V, not only measurable rectangles. All the integrals in the assumption and conclusion are extended nonnegative integrals with values in [0,+infinity]; equality of two infinite values is allowed.

No nonemptiness of A or B, positive mass, finite total mass, probability normalization, or countability or separation condition on the measurable spaces is assumed. Within the stated s-finiteness assumptions, the theorem includes mu = 0, R identically zero, F identically zero, and empty A or B. In the first two cases, and when either space is empty, pi is zero and the conclusion is trivial; when mu = 0 the almost-everywhere premise is vacuous, and when R is identically zero it holds automatically. When F is identically zero, K is zero and both sides of detailed balance vanish. Infinite total masses and infinite flux integrals are permitted. The premise need not hold for every a, and nothing is asserted about reversibility on exceptional a-fibers. The statement does not assert pointwise balance between individual states, existence of densities, Markov normalization, stationarity pi K = pi, irreducibility, uniqueness, or convergence.
scopes: The hypothesis places mu-almost every a outside the entire IsReversible property, so one null exceptional set works simultaneously for all measurable E,G. It is not a hypothesis only for each E,G with a potentially different exceptional set, and it is not an R(a)-almost-everywhere pointwise assertion about b. R(a) is the measure used in the fiber flux integrals. pi is the measure used in the conclusion. The conclusion is a global property for all measurable U,V. It adds no balance assertion on excluded a-fibers. Zero and empty cases obey the same scope; mu-null a-values contribute no pi mass even when fiber masses are infinite.
